content: 1. Please describe the type of healthcare setting in which you practice. Select all that apply: community clinic or health center, family planning clinic, health department, hospital-based clinic, private clinic, or other (please specify). 2. How many healthcare providers, including yourself, deliver family planning services in your practice or health center? Please provide the number. 3. What is your professional role as a healthcare provider? Select one: community health worker, nurse, nurse midwife, physician, or other (please specify). 4. On average, how many female patients of reproductive age do you see per week? Please provide the approximate number. 5. Have you received training in the insertion and removal of the following contraceptive methods for women during routine care? Indicate Yes or No for each: copper intrauterine device (Cu-IUD) and levonorgestrel-releasing intrauterine device (LNG-IUD). 6. Have you been trained in the insertion and removal of the following contraceptive methods for women immediately postpartum? Indicate Yes or No for each: copper intrauterine device (Cu-IUD) and levonorgestrel-releasing intrauterine device (LNG-IUD). 7. For each contraceptive method listed, indicate its availability in your practice or health center. Specify whether it is directly available onsite, prescribed/recommended for offsite access, patients are referred offsite to other providers, or it is not available. If unsure, select Don’t Know. Methods include LNG-IUD, Cu-IUD, implant, combined oral contraceptives (COCs), progestin-only oral pills (POPs), injectables (DMPA-IM, DMPA-SC, NET-EN), contraceptive patch, vaginal ring, diaphragm, male condom, female condom, emergency contraceptive pills, and Cu-IUD as emergency contraception. 8. In the past month, how often have you or your clinical team provided intrauterine devices (Cu-IUDs or LNG-IUDs) to nulliparous women? Select Very often, Often, Not often, or Never. If Not often or Never, please indicate the reasons. Reasons may include: rarely having nulliparous women as patients, unavailability of IUDs in your practice, concerns about safety for nulliparous women, concerns about effects on future fertility, difficulty with insertion, lack of training in IUD insertion, patient preference for other methods, practice protocols not allowing it, or other reasons (please specify). 9. Before initiating the following contraceptive methods, does your practice or health center require specific exams or tests for a healthy patient? Indicate for each method whether the following are required: blood pressure, weight, breast exam, pelvic exam, cervical cytology (Pap smear), STI risk assessment, or HIV screening. Methods include combined pills, progestogen-only pills, DMPA or NET-EN injections, implants, and intrauterine devices. If the method is not available in your practice, mark the appropriate box. 10. In the past year, when prescribing or providing combined hormonal contraceptives (COCs, patch, ring), how often did you initiate the method on the day of the patient’s visit regardless of the timing of her menses (Quick Start) if you were reasonably certain she was not pregnant? Please answer separately for adolescents and adults. Select Very often, Often, Not often, or Never. If Not often or Never, indicate the reasons, such as safety concerns, liability concerns, insufficient training, appropriateness for adolescents or adults, protocol restrictions, or other reasons (please specify). 11. In the past year, when providing DMPA or NET-EN injections, how often did you initiate the method on the day of the patient’s visit regardless of the timing of her menses (Quick Start) if you were reasonably certain she was not pregnant? Please answer separately for adolescents and adults. Select Very often, Often, Not often, or Never. If Not often or Never, indicate the reasons, such as safety concerns, liability concerns, insufficient training, appropriateness for adolescents or adults, protocol restrictions, or other reasons (please specify). 12. In the past year, when providing an intrauterine device (Cu-IUD or LNG-IUD), how often did you initiate the method on the day of the patient’s visit regardless of the timing of her menses (Quick Start) if you were reasonably certain she was not pregnant? Please answer separately for adolescents and adults. Select Very often, Often, Not often, or Never. If Not often or Never, indicate the reasons, such as unavailability of IUDs in your practice, safety concerns, liability concerns, insufficient training, appropriateness for adolescents or adults, protocol restrictions, or other reasons (please specify). 13. In the past year, when providing an implant, how often did you initiate the method on the day of the patient’s visit regardless of the timing of her menses (Quick Start) if you were reasonably certain she was not pregnant? Please answer separately for adolescents and adults. Select Very often, Often, Not often, or Never. If Not often or Never, indicate the reasons, such as unavailability of implants in your practice, safety concerns, liability concerns, insufficient training, appropriateness for adolescents or adults, protocol restrictions, or other reasons (please specify). 14. Do patients in your practice or health center routinely undergo a urine pregnancy test before starting a contraceptive method? Indicate Yes or No. 15. When can a woman initiate the following contraceptive methods? Check all applicable options for each method: oral contraceptives (all types), DMPA or NET-EN injection, implants, and intrauterine devices. Options include: any time as long as reasonably sure the woman is not pregnant, within 7 days after the start of normal menses, or on the same day after an abortion. 16. In the past month, how often have you been unable to provide a woman with her desired contraceptive method at the time of her visit? Select Very often, Often, Not often, or Never. If Very often or Often, indicate the reasons, such as unavailability of the chosen method, medical contraindications, inability to start the method due to timing of menses, concerns about potential pregnancy, need for further examinations or testing, lack of training in the chosen method, or other reasons (please specify). 17. In the past month, when counseling your typical female patient of reproductive age on family planning, how often have you or your clinical team done the following? Select Very often, Often, Not often, or Never for each: counseled on correct use of the contraceptive method, counseled on actions to take if a dose is late or missed, helped the patient identify and address potential barriers to correct use, counseled on possible changes in menstrual bleeding, counseled on return to fertility after discontinuing a method, counseled on discontinuing or switching methods, counseled on obtaining emergency contraception, and counseled on condom use for STD prevention.
